title: Deborah under the palm (Judges 4–5)
hook: a prophet and judge who leads an army and sings the victory song

segments.voice: Yesterday, the loop of Judges, and your word was judge: a deliverer, not a gavel. Where did you put your reminder to break the cycle? Day seven hundred three.

Between Ramah and Bethel, in the hill country of Ephraim, stands a palm tree with a name: the palm tree of Deborah. People come up to it with their disputes, and a woman sits beneath it and decides them. The King James gives her three descriptions in one line: "And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time." Israel is in the loop again. A Canaanite king, Jabin, has nine hundred chariots of iron, and the text says he has crushed them for twenty years. His general is Sisera. One day, Deborah sends for a man named Barak. Today: what she tells him, and the song she sings when it's over.

Deborah tells Barak that God commands him to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor, and God will draw Sisera out to meet him. Barak's answer is honest: "If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go." Readers argue over that line. Some hear hesitation. Others hear a man who knows where God's word is coming from and wants the prophet beside him. Deborah says yes, and adds a twist: the honor won't be his, "for the LORD shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman." On the day itself, she is the one who says go: "Up; for this is the day in which the LORD hath delivered Sisera into thine hand: is not the LORD gone out before thee?" Sisera's army breaks, and Sisera flees on foot to the tent of a woman named Jael, who kills him while he sleeps. So the woman of the prophecy isn't Deborah at all. It's Jael. Then, in chapter five, Deborah and Barak sing. It's a fierce poem. The stars fight from heaven; the river Kishon sweeps the enemy away. And in the middle of it, Deborah names herself. The villages had emptied, life on the roads had stopped, "until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel." A mother in Israel. The chapters never mention children of hers. She's a mother of a people: the one who got them up and moving again. The Bible calls her prophet and judge and gives no explanation for why a woman sits under the palm. She is simply there, and the people come up to her.
screen: `IS NOT THE LORD GONE OUT BEFORE THEE?`
`THE WOMAN IN THE PROPHECY IS JAEL.`
then, large: `I AROSE A MOTHER IN ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a woman leader you know. Settle, and breathe. Let one woman come to mind who got people up and moving: a grandmother who held a family together, a teacher, a manager, a nurse, a coach, the neighbor who organizes everyone. Someone people came to, the way they came up to the palm. See her face. What did she do that nobody thanked her for? Let your gratitude settle on that one specific thing. If you pray, you can give thanks for her by name. If you don't, simply hold her in mind and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Deborah. The prophet and judge Israel came up to under the palm tree: she called the battle, and she sang the song.
Your line: a mother in israel. Today, tell the woman you thought of, in a message or out loud, one specific thing she did that mattered. Day seven hundred three.

howItsDone: Deborah's story is told in Sunday schools and sermons as the story of a prophet and judge of Israel, and churches draw different conclusions from it about women's leadership in church today.

Judges 4:4: a prophetess, who judged Israel at that time.

fork.setup: you're Barak. a prophet tells you God commands you to gather an army against Sisera and his chariots of iron. what do you say?
options: only if you go with me.
fork.reveal: "If thou wilt go with me, then I will go." she goes, and tells him the honor will fall to a woman. it falls to Jael.

original.note: Hebrew: a mother in Israel, Deborah's name for herself in Judges 5:7.

trapdoor: what you thought: a battle story with a woman in a supporting role.
what it means: Deborah is prophet and judge; she calls the battle and sings the song, and another woman, Jael, ends it.
what a scholar hears: Judges 4 tells it in prose and Judges 5 in poetry, where she names herself em b'yisrael, a mother in Israel (5:7).
